transitionOut.text: Next: Aram's pressure and Joash on an Assyrian stele, Jeroboam II's Israel and the prophets Amos and Hosea, Tiglath-pileser III, the fall of Damascus and Galilee, the siege and fall of Samaria, the exile of its people, and Judah left alone.

events.title: Joash the Samarian
events.text: Around 796 BC Adad-nirari III of Assyria marched west and took a great tribute from the king of Damascus. A stele found at Tell al-Rimah in northern Iraq in 1967 lists another king who paid: 'Joash the Samarian'. He is Jehu's grandson, the king who, says the Bible, won back Israel's towns from Aram.
events.why: It ties a king of the Bible to an Assyrian text, and shows the pattern of the century: when Assyria struck Damascus, Israel could breathe again. Assyria now names Israel after its capital, Samaria.
claims: Tribute of Joash (Iu'asu) the Samarian on the Tell al-Rimah stele of Adad-nirari III.
Hazael and his son oppress Israel; a 'deliverer'; Joash wins back the towns: 2 Kings 13.
Assyria's campaigns against Damascus gave Israel room to recover.

events.title: Jeroboam II: oil, wine and a lion seal
events.text: The Bible gives Jeroboam II 41 years and a border from Lebo-hamath to the Dead Sea, in just a few verses. At Samaria, the Harvard expedition found over a hundred inscribed sherds, the Samaria Ostraca, recording wine and oil sent to the capital. At Megiddo in 1904, a jasper seal with a roaring lion was found, reading 'belonging to Shema, servant of Jeroboam'.
events.why: Israel Finkelstein sees these years as the peak of the northern kingdom. The ostraca's personal names, some built with Yahu and some with Baal, give a rare glimpse of ordinary faith.
claims: Jeroboam II reigns 41 years and restores the border: 2 Kings 14:23–29.
The Samaria Ostraca record deliveries of wine and oil; names with Yahu and Baal.
The ostraca date to the first half of the 8th century BC.
The Shema seal, found in 1904, is lost and known from casts; its 'Jeroboam' is probably Jeroboam II.
The 8th century BC as the peak of the northern kingdom.

events.title: Amos and Hosea
events.text: Amos, a herdsman from Tekoa in Judah, speaks at the royal shrine of Bethel against those who 'lie on beds of ivory' while the poor are crushed: 'Let justice roll down like waters'. Hosea, from the north, speaks of Israel as an unfaithful wife whom God still loves. Their books are among the oldest of the prophets.
events.why: Their words, against wealth without justice and faith without loyalty, became part of the Hebrew Bible and are still read in synagogues today. Ivory inlays like those Amos condemns were found at Samaria.
claims: Amos at Bethel; beds of ivory; 'Let justice roll down': Amos 1:1; 5:24; 6:4–6; 7:10–15.
Hosea's marriage and God's love: Hosea 1–3; 11.
Yadin linked a destruction at Hazor with the earthquake of Amos 1:1.

events.title: Tiglath-pileser III names three kings
events.text: Tiglath-pileser III made the conquered lands into provinces and moved whole peoples. His annals and lists of tribute name Menahem of Samaria, Jehoahaz (Ahaz) of Judah, and Pekah, whom 'they overthrew', and Hoshea, whom 'I set as king over them'. In Babylon he ruled under the name Pulu, the 'Pul' of the Bible.
events.why: For the first time, Assyrian texts and the Book of Kings can be read almost year by year side by side. Each king of Israel and Judah had to choose between paying Assyria and resisting it.
claims: Menahem of Samaria, Jehoahaz of Judah, Pekah and Hoshea in Tiglath-pileser III's inscriptions.
His policy of provinces and two-way deportations.
Menahem pays Pul a thousand talents; Ahaz: 'I am your servant and your son': 2 Kings 15:19–20; 16:7–8.
Rezin and Pekah against Ahaz; the sign of Immanuel: Isaiah 7.

events.title: 732 BC: Damascus, Galilee and Hazor
events.text: After campaigns 'to Damascus' in 733 and 732 BC, Tiglath-pileser took Damascus and made Aram a province. Israel lost Galilee and Gilead. At Hazor, the city of this time ended in fire under a thick layer of ash. The Bible names the towns taken, from Ijon to Hazor, and says their people were carried off to Assyria.
events.why: Within a few years the northern kingdom shrank to the hills around Samaria. It was the first great deportation of Israelites.
claims: Hazor Stratum V destroyed by fire, with a thick ash layer, in 732 BC.
Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee and Naphtali taken and deported: 2 Kings 15:29.

events.title: Who took Samaria?
events.text: The Bible says Shalmaneser V besieged Samaria for three years and took it. A Babylonian chronicle says only that Shalmaneser 'ravaged Shamara'in'. His successor Sargon II claims the conquest for himself: '27,290 people' in his palace at Khorsabad, '27,280' and 200 chariots on a prism from Nimrud. In 720 BC Samaria joined a revolt led by Hamath, which Sargon crushed at Qarqar.
events.why: Hayim Tadmor proposed that Samaria was taken twice, by Shalmaneser in 722 and again by Sargon in 720 BC, and many follow him. On the summit itself, Ron Tappy found little sign of a great burning.
claims: The siege of three years: 2 Kings 17:5–6; 18:9–10.
Sargon's Khorsabad inscriptions: Samaria conquered, 27,290 deported, 50 chariots.
The Nimrud Prism: 27,280 deported and 200 chariots; Samaria resettled 'greater than before'.
The revolt of 720 BC crushed at Qarqar.
No clear destruction layer on the summit.

events.title: Carried off: Israel in Assyria
events.text: The Bible says Israel was settled 'in Halah, on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes'. Assyrian documents bear it out: Israelite names, built with the name of Israel's God, appear in the following decades at Gozan, Kalhu and other cities, and a unit of Samarian charioteers served in the Assyrian army.
events.why: Scholars think many Israelites stayed on the land; Assyria's own figure covers only part of the population. But those who were taken away mostly vanish from history, and that became the tradition of the ten lost tribes.
claims: Halah, Habor, Gozan and the cities of the Medes: 2 Kings 17:6.
Israelite names in Assyrian documents after 720 BC.
Samarian charioteers in the Nimrud Horse Lists.
The deportations were partial; many stayed.

events.title: The Samaritans and the ten tribes
events.text: The Bible says Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Hamath and other places to Samaria, and that they learned to fear the God of the land from a priest at Bethel. Later Jewish writings call the Samaritans 'Kutim'. The Samaritans tell a different story: they are Israelites who never left, keepers of the Torah on Mount Gerizim. A small community still lives there today.
events.why: Jewish tradition remembers the exiles as the ten lost tribes. Rabbi Akiva taught in the Mishnah that they would not return; others hoped they would. The same events gave rise to two traditions that still live.
claims: Settlers from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath and Sepharvaim; the priest at Bethel: 2 Kings 17:24–28.
Sargon settled conquered peoples, and later Arabs, in Samaria.
Samaritan self-understanding; 'Kutim'; Mount Gerizim; the community today.
Rabbi Akiva: the ten tribes will not return (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:3).
Traditions of the ten lost tribes.

events.title: Jerusalem grows
events.text: In the late 8th century BC Jerusalem spread from the old City of David onto the western hill and grew several times over. Magen Broshi and Israel Finkelstein linked the growth with refugees from the fallen north. Nadav Na'aman argues it had other causes and began later.
events.why: Whatever its cause, Jerusalem became Judah's great city just as Israel disappeared, and the traditions of the north, carried south, became part of Judah's story.
claims: Jerusalem's growth onto the western hill, late 8th century BC.
Refugees from the north as the cause.
Hezekiah invites Ephraim and Manasseh to the Passover: 2 Chronicles 30.

claims: Assyrian documents bear this out. Names built with the name of Israel's God turn up in the following years at Gozan, at Kalhu, and in other cities of Assyria.

steps.text: At Kalhu, lists of the royal army name a unit of Samarian charioteers, serving the king of Assyria.
claims: At Kalhu, lists of the royal army name a unit of Samarian charioteers, serving the king of Assyria.

vignette.alt: Two-horse chariots with drivers and archers parading before high mudbrick walls, horses with plumes and tassels
vignette.caption: Assyrian chariots (impression)

steps.label: New settlers for Samaria (tradition and Assyrian texts)

steps.text: In their place, the Bible says, Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath and Sepharvaim, and settled them in the towns of Samaria.
claims: In their place, the Bible says, Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath and Sepharvaim, and settled them in the towns of Samaria.

steps.text: Sargon's own words agree. He says he settled people from the lands he had conquered there, and later Arab tribes from the desert.
claims: Sargon's own words agree. He says he settled people from the lands he had conquered there, and later Arab tribes from the desert.

steps.text: How many left? Assyria's own figure is only a part of the kingdom's people. K. Lawson Younger and others think many Israelites stayed on the land.
claims: How many left? Assyria's own figure is only a part of the kingdom's people. K. Lawson Younger and others think many Israelites stayed on the land.

steps.text: The Bible explains the fall in a long sermon. Israel had served other gods, and would not listen to the prophets.
claims: The Bible explains the fall in a long sermon. Israel had served other gods, and would not listen to the prophets.

steps.text: It tells how the new settlers feared the God of the land, and were taught by an Israelite priest sent back to Bethel.
claims: It tells how the new settlers feared the God of the land, and were taught by an Israelite priest sent back to Bethel.

steps.text: Later Jewish writings call the Samaritans Kutim, people from Cuthah. The Samaritans tell their own story. They descend, they say, from Israelites who never left, and their holy mountain is Gerizim.
claims: Later Jewish writings call the Samaritans Kutim, people from Cuthah. The Samaritans tell their own story. They descend, they say, from Israelites who never left, and their holy mountain is Gerizim.

vignette.alt: A line of robed pilgrims climbing a winding path up a green rocky mountain among olive trees
vignette.caption: Mount Gerizim (impression)

steps.text: A small Samaritan community still lives there today.
claims: A small Samaritan community still lives there today.

steps.text: And Jewish tradition remembers the ten lost tribes, carried away and never seen again. Rabbi Akiva taught that they would not return.
claims: And Jewish tradition remembers the ten lost tribes, carried away and never seen again. Rabbi Akiva taught that they would not return.

steps.text: Imagine a family in Gozan, far from the hills of Samaria, giving their child a name with the name of Israel's God in it.

vignette.alt: A mother kneading bread by a mudbrick house and a father mending a net by a river, a child watching the water, a mound in the distance
vignette.caption: By the Khabur (impression)

steps.text: In the south, Judah survives, as a vassal of Assyria. Sargon calls himself the subduer of Judah, which lies far away.
claims: In the south, Judah survives, as a vassal of Assyria. Sargon calls himself the subduer of Judah, which lies far away.

steps.text: Jerusalem grows fast in these years, onto the western hill. Some archaeologists think refugees from the north came with it. Nadav Na'aman doubts it.
claims: Jerusalem grows fast in these years, onto the western hill. Some archaeologists think refugees from the north came with it. Nadav Na'aman doubts it.

vignette.alt: Workers building a thick new stone wall around a crowded hillside town while people with bundles arrive on the road
vignette.caption: Jerusalem grows (impression)

steps.text: The Bible says Judah's next king, Hezekiah, sent letters to the north as well, inviting Ephraim and Manasseh to keep the Passover in Jerusalem.
claims: The Bible says Judah's next king, Hezekiah, sent letters to the north as well, inviting Ephraim and Manasseh to keep the Passover in Jerusalem.

steps.text: But Assyria is not done with Judah. In seven oh one BC, a new king, Sennacherib, will march on Jerusalem. That is where our next chapter begins.
claims: In seven oh one BC, a new king, Sennacherib, will march on Jerusalem.
